summary: This RFC introduces four schemes for per-packet authentication, integrity, and anti-replay in ALC and NORM multicast protocols. They use RSA signatures, ECDSA, and a group-keyed message authentication code, among others.

plainLanguage.summary: When one sender talks to a big group, each message needs a seal to prove it is real. This gives four ways to apply the seal.

questions: how to authenticate alc and norm packets
subtitle: Four ways to authenticate every packet of ALC and NORM multicast sessions, using signatures, a group-keyed MAC, or both.

tldr.problem: In ALC and NORM multicast sessions, an attacker might impersonate the sender and inject forged packets, corrupting what receivers reconstruct, or forge feedback to a NORM sender.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet carries an EXT_AUTH header extension with an ASID field naming the scheme: an RSA signature, an ECDSA signature, a group-keyed MAC, or a signature protected by a MAC. Optional anti-replay uses a sequence number.
tldr.outcome: Operators can pick a scheme to suit data rate and threat model, and mix schemes in one session. The group MAC cannot stop an attack from a group member.

facts.label: Default truncated MAC in combined scheme

today: RFC 6584 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The TESLA-based alternative for the same protocols is described in RFC 5776.

sections.title: Why Multicast Packets Need Authentication
sections.content:
ALC (RFC 5775) and NORM (RFC 5740) are content delivery protocols that reliably move objects such as files from a sender to many receivers. NORM uses bidirectional transmissions: receivers acknowledge data or ask for retransmission. ALC is unidirectional and relies on cyclic transmission in a carousel, proactive forward error correction, or both.

An attacker might impersonate the session sender and inject forged packets, corrupting the objects receivers rebuild. In NORM an attacker might also forge feedback packets to the sender. This RFC provides per-packet authentication, integrity and anti-replay services against both.

It specifies four schemes: RSA digital signatures, ECDSA, a group-keyed Message Authentication Code (MAC), and a combination of signature and group MAC. TESLA is covered separately in RFC 5776. Unlike TESLA, this document also authenticates packets sent by NORM receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can slip fake letters into the mail to a big group, people could be fooled. Each letter needs a stamp that proves who sent it.

sections.title: Choosing Between the Schemes
sections.content:
The RFC compares the approaches. Digital signatures suit low data rate flows and prove who sent a packet, but RSA has high computational cost and transmission overhead. ECC relaxes this: a 1024-bit RSA key and a 160-bit ECC key give equivalent security, as do a 2048-bit RSA key and a 224-bit ECC key. RSA loads the signer more and the verifier much less, while ECC loads both about equally.

A group-keyed MAC suits high data rate flows where overhead must be minimal, but it cannot protect against a group member who impersonates the sender. TESLA gives sender authentication with low overhead but is more complex, needs loosely synchronized clocks, and delays authentication until a key is disclosed.
sections.plainLanguage: A fancy personal stamp is very safe but slow and bulky. A shared club password is fast, but any club member could fake it.

sections.title: The EXT_AUTH Header Extension
sections.content:
All schemes use the HET=1 (EXT_AUTH) header extension from RFC 5651. The 4-bit ASID (Authentication Scheme IDentifier) tells a receiver how to read it, so several schemes can coexist in one session, up to a maximum of 16. The ASID-to-scheme association is set at session startup and communicated out-of-band, and it is scoped per session.

The signature-based and MAC-based formats add these fields after HET and HEL: ASID (4 bits), rsvd (3 bits, set to zero), AR (1 bit, anti-replay used or not), SN (8 bits set to zero when AR is 0, or a 40-bit Sequence Number when AR is 1), then the signature or MAC, padded with zeros to a multiple of 32 bits.

Worked examples: a 1024-bit RSA signature (128 bytes) without anti-replay makes a header extension of 132 bytes with HEL=33. ECDSA-256 makes it 36 bytes with HEL=9. HMAC-SHA-256 with a 16-byte MAC makes it 16 bytes with HEL=4.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet gets a small label that says which kind of seal is used, then a counter number, then the seal itself.

sections.title: RSA, ECDSA and Group-Keyed MAC Schemes
sections.content:
For RSA signatures, the sender MUST communicate a public key, the signature-encoding algorithm (for example RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 or RSASSA-PSS), the hash function (SHA-256 is RECOMMENDED), and whether anti-replay is used. Key sizes between 1024 and 2048 bits inclusive are RECOMMENDED, and sizes below 1024 SHOULD NOT be used. The signature covers the ALC or NORM header with its extensions and the payload, but not UDP/IP headers, and the Signature field is zero during computation.

For ECDSA, the RFC lists ECDSA-256 (SHA-256, secp256r1), ECDSA-384 (SHA-384, secp384r1) and ECDSA-521 (SHA-512, secp521r1). ECDSA-256 with secp256r1 is the default and RECOMMENDED choice.

For the group-keyed MAC, all senders and receivers share a group key, delivered confidentially before the session. The MAC (for example HMAC-SHA-256, which is RECOMMENDED) is truncated to its n_m leftmost bits. A receiver recomputes it and MUST drop the packet on mismatch.

In every scheme, each packet MUST carry exactly one matching EXT_AUTH extension, and receivers MUST drop packets without one. Receivers that cannot parse the scheme's contents ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: One way uses a private pen that only the sender owns. Another uses a shared secret handshake known to the whole group.

sections.title: Anti-Replay Processing
sections.content:
Anti-replay follows the sequence number approach of RFC 4303, but with a 40-bit field holding all bits of the counter. The sender starts its counter at 0 and increments it for each packet, so the first packet carries 1. The sequence number is set before the signature is computed, so it is protected by it. The RFC notes that on a 10-Gbps network with 64-byte packets, the counter would cycle after slightly more than 15 hours.

The receiver first checks that the number does not duplicate any earlier one, using a sliding window. If this check fails, the packet is discarded without any cryptographic work. If it passes, the receiver verifies integrity and only then updates its window. A packet failing integrity MUST be discarded as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet is numbered. If the same number shows up twice, it is a copy, so it gets thrown away.

sections.title: Combining a Signature with a Group MAC
sections.content:
The combined scheme adds a light group-keyed MAC as a front end to a signature, to blunt denial-of-service attacks from outsiders. The sender computes the signature, stores it, then computes the MAC over the packet including the signature. A receiver checks the MAC first and drops the packet if it fails, and only then checks the signature.

Anti-replay MUST be used with this scheme. Otherwise replayed but valid packets would pass the cheap MAC check and force expensive signature verification. The AR bit is always 1.

The limits are stated plainly. The MAC does not help if a group member impersonates the sender. It adds a MAC computation for every packet at both ends and enlarges the header. So n_m MUST be a multiple of 32 bits, with a default of 32 bits. A 32-bit MAC gives a one in 2^32 chance of a packet being forged, which the RFC considers acceptable because the signature check still follows. With a 128-byte signature, the combined extension is 140 bytes with HEL=35.
sections.plainLanguage: A quick guard at the door checks the club password first. Only people who pass get the slower, careful ID check inside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Signatures create a new denial-of-service opportunity: forged packets are cheap to make but costly to check, so an attacker can saturate a receiver. The RFC RECOMMENDS the combined scheme as a mitigation, though nothing helps against an attacking group member. It also RECOMMENDS limiting the number of authentication checks per time unit once failures pass a threshold.

Anti-replay is RECOMMENDED for the signature and MAC schemes and required for the combined one. For NORM, the 16-bit sequence field could only serve for anti-replay if at most 65535 packets are sent, and a host in several sessions should change its instance_id for each. For ALC, replayed data symbols and the close flags are harmless, timing information in EXT_TIME may be sensitive, and the TSI MUST be changed for each session.

The parameters sent out-of-band, especially the ASID mapping, are critical and SHOULD be carried in a secure way.
sections.plainLanguage: Fake packets are easy to make but slow to check, so guards should have a quick test first and stop checking if too many fakes arrive.

fields.desc: Identifies the authentication scheme in use.

fields.name: rsvd
fields.desc: Reserved; set to zero and ignored by receivers.

fields.name: AR
fields.desc: Whether the anti-replay service is used.

fields.name: SN
fields.desc: 8 bits set to zero when AR is 0, or a 40-bit sequence number when AR is 1.
